Empirical Research Plan – “Bank Branch Expansion, Poverty and Rural Output in India, 1961-2000”

------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------
Preferred design: Difference-in-differences (DID) with an event-study extension, instrumented where needed by the interaction of the post-policy period with a state’s pre-policy share of rural unbanked locations (“social-banking exposure IV”).

Why DID?  
• Variation is sharp in time (1969 nationalisation, 1977 1:4 rule, repeal in 1990) and heterogeneous across states in intensity (states that were financially backward in 1961 were forced to open many more rural branches).  
• We observe a long state-year panel, allowing state and year fixed effects to soak up level differences and nationwide shocks.  
• A transparent event-study illustrates pre-trends.  
• IV deals with the remaining concern that branch placement could still respond to contemporaneous poverty/wage changes.

Formal estimating equation (reduced form):

Y_st = α + β POST_t × LOWFD_s  + γ_s + δ_t + θX_st + ε_st              (1)

where  
POST_t = 1 for 1969–1990 (or 1977–1990 in a tighter specification);  
LOWFD_s = 1 if 1961 rural branches per capita below national median;  
β is the DID effect of the programme on outcome Y (poverty rate, wages, output share).  

Second-stage IV:

ΔBranches_pc_st  = π POST_t × LOWFD_s + γ_s + δ_t + θX_st + u_st        (2)  
Y_st  = α + λ \hat{ΔBranches_pc_st} + γ_s + δ_t + θX_st + η_st         (3)  

λ gives the causal effect of an additional rural branch per 100,000 people.

------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
– Main: Annual change in rural bank branches per 100,000 population in state s at time t (ΔBranches_pc_st).  
– Binary DID variant: POST_t × LOWFD_s.

Control group  
– States with above-median 1961 rural branch density (financially developed) form the counterfactual trend.  

Treatment timing  
– Baseline “post” begins 1969; robustness narrow post = 1977–1990 to isolate the 1:4 rule.  

Running variable / cutoff  
– Not an RDD, so not applicable.

------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the social-banking mandate, poverty, wages and output shares in low- and high-FD states would have evolved in parallel.  
 Plausibility: Reasonable because before 1969 branch expansion was commercially driven and slow in both sets; can be checked with pre-1969 event-study coefficients.  

A2. Exogeneity of initial financial development: 1961 branch density is predetermined and not itself caused by impending poverty changes in the 1970s/80s.  
 Plausibility: Branch penetration in 1961 largely reflects colonial rail lines and princely-state banking rules, unlikely to predict differential poverty trends decades later conditional on covariates.  

A3. No interference (SUTVA): A rural branch opened in state s primarily affects outcomes in s, not neighbouring states.  
 Plausibility: Inter-state migration and credit flows were limited by language and priority-sector lending requirements; still, we will cluster SEs at the state level and test spillovers.  

A4. Stable policy environment for other anti-poverty programmes after controlling for observed covariates.  
 Plausibility: We control for land reforms, public food distribution, and state expenditure; residual correlation should be small.

------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
------------------------------------------------
T1. Simultaneous pro-poor policies (land reforms, PDS expansion) happen more in low-FD states.  
  • Include time-varying state controls for land-reform enactment, PDS coverage, and government expenditure shares.  
  • Add state-specific linear trends.  

T2. Mean reversion / convergence: poorer states (also low-FD) would have experienced faster poverty decline anyway.  
  • Event-study plots of β_τ for each pre-policy year; flat pre-trend supports DID.  
  • Placebo re-assign treatment to 1950s and re-estimate.  

T3. Endogenous branch placement within the policy: although the 1:4 rule constrained banks, they still chose which unbanked villages to enter.  
  • Instrument actual branch openings with policy exposure (POST_t × LOWFD_s) as outlined.  
  • Add district-level robustness (if data permit) to exploit even finer exogenous targeting lists produced by Lead Banks.

------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)    # fast data handling
library(fixest)        # high-dimensional FE
library(ivreg)         # IV estimation
library(ggplot2)       # plots

# 1. Load data --------------------------------------------------------------
dt  <- fread("state_year_panel_1961_2000.csv")  # one row per state-year

# 2. Variable construction --------------------------------------------------
dt[, post69 := year >= 1969]
dt[, post77 := year >= 1977 & year <= 1990]     # narrower post for robustness
# Low initial financial development (1961 branches per capita below median)
median_fd <- dt[year == 1961, median(rural_branches_pc)]
dt[, lowFD := (rural_branches_pc[year==1961][.I] < median_fd), by = state]

# DID interaction
dt[, did69 := post69 * lowFD]
dt[, did77 := post77 * lowFD]

# Outcomes
# poverty_rural, ag_wage_real, sdp_primary_share already in data

# 3. Main DID specification -------------------------------------------------
# Example for rural poverty
did_pov <- feols(poverty_rural ~ did69 + land_reform + pds_coverage + 
                 state_expenditure_share | state + year,
                 data = dt, cluster = ~state)
summary(did_pov)

# 4. Event-study ------------------------------------------------------------
dt[, rel_year := year - 1969]   # event time wrt 1969
est <- feols(poverty_rural ~ i(rel_year, lowFD, -5:20) + land_reform + pds_coverage |
             state + year, data = dt, cluster = ~state)
iplot(est, ref.line = 0) + theme_minimal()

# 5. IV approach ------------------------------------------------------------
iv_pov <- ivreg(poverty_rural ~ delta_branches_pc + land_reform + pds_coverage |
                post69:lowFD + land_reform + pds_coverage + state + year,
                data = dt)
summary(iv_pov, diagnostics = TRUE)

# 6. Robustness check: alternate post window -------------------------------
did_pov77 <- feols(poverty_rural ~ did77 + land_reform + pds_coverage |
                   state + year, data = dt, cluster = ~state)
etable(did_pov, did_pov77, tex = FALSE)
```

------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts that improved access to formal credit and savings smoothes consumption, finances input purchases, and shifts labour out of agriculture.

Priors:  
– Rural poverty headcount: decline of roughly 3–5 percentage points per 100 additional rural branches (≈one s.d. of expansion).  
– Real male agricultural wages: increase by 5–8 %.  
– Output structure: primary sector share falls by ~2 pp; tertiary rises by ~1.5 pp; secondary by ~0.5 pp.

------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
------------------------------------------------
C1. Pre-trend equality checked with event-study ………………… 1  
C2. No anticipation before 1969 ………………………………………… 0.8 (possible modest anticipation 1968)  
C3. No contemporaneous confounders unaccounted for ……… 0.7  
C4. No spillovers across states ………………………………………… 0.8  
C5. Correct inference & clustering …………………………………… 1  

Overall (sum/5) ≈ 4.3 / 5 – reasonably strong but not bullet-proof.

------------------------------------------------
This plan leverages India’s unique social-banking mandate as a quasi-experiment, combines DID with an exposure-based instrument, and embeds extensive falsification and robustness tests to support causal inference on rural poverty and economic transformation.
